subject: WAIC/LOO calculations in a regression model with prediction

messages.author: c48a384dbad0597c
messages.subject: WAIC/LOO calculations in a regression model with prediction
parts:
Dear All,

I am trying to build a linear regression model using a t distribution after standardizing the data (the code and data are attached, also nimbleCode is shown below). To build the model using NIMBLE, I have adapted a regression model from Kruschke's DBDA written in JAGS (I migrated from JAGS to NIMBLE).

For model evaluation, I calculated WAIC and LOO values using the loo package based on "logProb_", i.e., I added "logProb_" for monitoring (please see the code attached). To make sure that I get the correct WAIC and LOO values, I wrote a JAGS code and computed those values to be compared with NIMBLE. I found those values are almost identical to each other assuring me those values are correct.

The problem is that when I added a node for predicted values (for this testing, I use the same predictors for predictions, i.e., all (zx==zx_pred) is TRUE), the WAIC and LOO values from NIMBLE is totally different from those without the prediction (i.e., original one). At this point, even the log likelihood values are strange (maybe I made a mistake while debugging). For the predicted values, I used a truncation function since the values should be > 0. Of course, I did this prediction part in R after MCMC, but I wanted to do inside NIMBLE, in particular when I see the huge discrepancy in WAIC/LOO values after adding the prediction node. 

I really wonder what's going on there.

Any help would be appreciated.

- Seongeun

---------------------



rm (list=ls())

library (loo)

library (nimble)

set.seed(9999)


mc_model <- nimbleCode({

for ( i in 1:N) {

zy[i] ~ dt( zbeta0 + sum( zbeta[1:Nx] * zx[i,1:Nx]), sigma = z_sigma, df = df_n )

}

# Vague priors

zbeta0 ~ dnorm( 0 , sd = 2) 

for ( j in 1:Nx ) {

zbeta[j] ~ dnorm( 0 , sd =2 )

}

z_sigma ~ T(dt(mu = 0, sigma = 1, df=1), 1e-5, 10)

df_n ~ dexp(1/30.0)

# Transform to original scale:

beta[1:Nx] <- ( zbeta[1:Nx] / x_sd[1:Nx] )*y_sd

beta0 <- zbeta0*y_sd  + y_m - sum( zbeta[1:Nx] * x_m[1:Nx] / x_sd[1:Nx] )*y_sd

sigma <- z_sigma*y_sd

# Predicted y values

# For now, use the original predictors

if (PREDICT_Y) {

for ( i in 1:N_pred ) {

# y_sd and y_m are both >0, so zyP SHOULD > 0

zy_p[i] ~ T(dt( zbeta0 + sum( zbeta[1:Nx] * zx_pred[i,1:Nx] ), sigma = z_sigma , df=df_n), 0, )

#zy_p[i] ~ dt( zbeta0 + sum( zbeta[1:Nx] * zx_pred[i,1:Nx] ), sigma = z_sigma , df=df_n)#

y_pred[i] <- zy_p[i] * y_sd + y_m

}

}

})


PREDICT_Y = TRUE


params = c( "beta0" ,  "beta" ,  "sigma", 

"zbeta0" , "zbeta" , "z_sigma", "df_n", "logProb_zy")


load ('input.RData')


N = length (Data$zy)


model <- nimbleModel(code=mc_model, data = Data, 

constants= Const, init=Inits)


Cmodel <- compileNimble(model)


if (PREDICT_Y) {

modelConf <- configureMCMC(model, print = TRUE, thin = 1, 

monitors = params, monitors2 = 'y_pred')

} else {

modelConf <- configureMCMC(model, print = TRUE, thin = 1, 

monitors = params)

}

modelMCMC <- buildMCMC(modelConf)

CmodelMCMC <- compileNimble(modelMCMC, project = model)


niter <- 1e4


CmodelMCMC$run(niter)

samples = as.matrix(CmodelMCMC$mvSamples)[5000:10000,]


if (PREDICT_Y) {

yp_samples = as.matrix(CmodelMCMC$mvSamples2)[5000:10000,]

}


#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Log likelihood for WAIC & LOO

#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

ll <- samples[,paste0("logProb_zy[",1:N,"]")]


waic_res = loo::waic (as.matrix (ll))

loo_res = loo::loo (as.matrix (ll))

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: WAIC/LOO calculations in a regression model with prediction
parts:
Hi Seongjeun,

Thanks for the question.

It looks like with PREDICT_Y == TRUE, there is no mixing at all in the model.  I may not be following everything, but it looks like this occurs because Inits$z_sigma is 0, which means all zy_p[i] values are 0 and have logProb_zy_p[i] of Inf, and all logProb_zy[i] are -Inf.  The sampling is never able to get away from this state.  

When PREDICT_Y == FALSE, the initial states still have z_sigma == 0 and all logProb_zy[i] are -Inf.  However, any non-zero value of z_sigma in the first MCMC iteration would be accepted because it would raise the logProb_zy[i] to real values and hence be an infinite improvement.  When PREDICT_Y == TRUE, I think this would be defeated by the logProb_zy_p[i] values of Inf, which would make any change in z_sigma give infinitely worse fit. 

In any case, can you try initializing z_sigma with a value > 0?

It still may not be a good idea to include stochastic posterior predictive nodes, because they will slow your mixing.  One strategy for posterior prediction is to make another nimbleModel for that purpose.  You would then iterate over the posterior sample from the first model, put each set of states into the posterior prediction model, and use it for simulation as needed.  Of course in a simple case like yours, you could also do it more directly.  If you use the mvSamples directly, you can access variables in it by name.

Perry

messages.subject: Re: WAIC/LOO calculations in a regression model with prediction
parts:
Hi Perry,

I appreciate your time looking at my question and running the code.

Your insight was absoluately correct. The problem was in setting Inits$z_sigma to 0. Now I get a very similar LOO IC value between with and without the predictive node.

> loo_res

Computed from 5001 by 271 log-likelihood matrix

         Estimate   SE
elpd_loo   -266.6 19.9
p_loo         8.8  0.9
looic       533.3 39.8
------
Monte Carlo SE of elpd_loo is 0.1.

Pareto k diagnostic values:
                         Count Pct.    Min. n_eff
(-Inf, 0.5]   (good)     270   99.6%   3153
 (0.5, 0.7]   (ok)         1    0.4%   646
   (0.7, 1]   (bad)        0    0.0%   <NA>
   (1, Inf)   (very bad)   0    0.0%   <NA>

All Pareto k estimates are ok (k < 0.7).

In this standardized data, I naively thought z_sigma can be a very small number and set it to 0 as an initial guess. I didn't realize the mixing is this sensitive to the initial values - a different experience from JAGS??. The reason I didn't suspect the initial value as the source of the problem was that when I didn't provide the initial value for z_sigma (i.e., let NIMBLE figure it out) at least there was no Inf value. 

With respect to the slow mixing with the prediction node inside the model, I didn't see signs of slow mixing. I often used predictive nodes inside the model in JAGS, but didn't see a problem. That's probably because my models were simple. 

The idea of using another nimbleModel seems to be good. I guess this is one of the advantages of NIMBLE over other MCMC software.  

This is a simple model relative to my previous other ones, but I think here I was able to calculate WAIC/LOO information criteria from log likelihood from NIMBLE (please let me know it if this is not the correct way although I checked with JAGS and find similar results). I guess this gives me some flexibility in model selection/variable selection using NIMBLE.

Again, thank you so much for your valuable help.

- Seongeun

parts:
Thanks for the follow-up.

While I'm not sure about this particular case, I can say there are cases where NIMBLE benefits more (i.e. is more sensitive) from useful initial values than does JAGS.  To some extent, this has to do with which samplers are used.

Also I should note that NIMBLE does have its own WAIC method that can be enabled by an argument to configureMCMC.  I'd be curious if it matches what you get from the loo package.

On Thursday, June 7, 2018 at 5:18:13 AM UTC-7, pdevalpine wrote:
Hi Seongjeun,

Thanks for the question.

It looks like with PREDICT_Y == TRUE, there is no mixing at all in the model.  I may not be following everything, but it looks like this occurs because Inits$z_sigma is 0, which means all zy_p[i] values are 0 and have logProb_zy_p[i] of Inf, and all logProb_zy[i] are -Inf.  The sampling is never able to get away from this state.  

When PREDICT_Y == FALSE, the initial states still have z_sigma == 0 and all logProb_zy[i] are -Inf.  However, any non-zero value of z_sigma in the first MCMC iteration would be accepted because it would raise the logProb_zy[i] to real values and hence be an infinite improvement.  When PREDICT_Y == TRUE, I think this would be defeated by the logProb_zy_p[i] values of Inf, which would make any change in z_sigma give infinitely worse fit. 

In any case, can you try initializing z_sigma with a value > 0?

It still may not be a good idea to include stochastic posterior predictive nodes, because they will slow your mixing.  One strategy for posterior prediction is to make another nimbleModel for that purpose.  You would then iterate over the posterior sample from the first model, put each set of states into the posterior prediction model, and use it for simulation as needed.  Of course in a simple case like yours, you could also do it more directly.  If you use the mvSamples directly, you can access variables in it by name.

Perry

Dear All,

I am trying to build a linear regression model using a t distribution after standardizing the data (the code and data are attached, also nimbleCode is shown below). To build the model using NIMBLE, I have adapted a regression model from Kruschke's DBDA written in JAGS (I migrated from JAGS to NIMBLE).

For model evaluation, I calculated WAIC and LOO values using the loo package based on "logProb_", i.e., I added "logProb_" for monitoring (please see the code attached). To make sure that I get the correct WAIC and LOO values, I wrote a JAGS code and computed those values to be compared with NIMBLE. I found those values are almost identical to each other assuring me those values are correct.

The problem is that when I added a node for predicted values (for this testing, I use the same predictors for predictions, i.e., all (zx==zx_pred) is TRUE), the WAIC and LOO values from NIMBLE is totally different from those without the prediction (i.e., original one). At this point, even the log likelihood values are strange (maybe I made a mistake while debugging). For the predicted values, I used a truncation function since the values should be > 0. Of course, I did this prediction part in R after MCMC, but I wanted to do inside NIMBLE, in particular when I see the huge discrepancy in WAIC/LOO values after adding the prediction node. 

I really wonder what's going on there.

Any help would be appreciated.

- Seongeun

---------------------



rm (list=ls())

library (loo)

library (nimble)

set.seed(9999)


mc_model <- nimbleCode({

for ( i in 1:N) {

zy[i] ~ dt( zbeta0 + sum( zbeta[1:Nx] * zx[i,1:Nx]), sigma = z_sigma, df = df_n )

}

# Vague priors

zbeta0 ~ dnorm( 0 , sd = 2) 

for ( j in 1:Nx ) {

zbeta[j] ~ dnorm( 0 , sd =2 )

}

z_sigma ~ T(dt(mu = 0, sigma = 1, df=1), 1e-5, 10)

df_n ~ dexp(1/30.0)

# Transform to original scale:

beta[1:Nx] <- ( zbeta[1:Nx] / x_sd[1:Nx] )*y_sd

beta0 <- zbeta0*y_sd  + y_m - sum( zbeta[1:Nx] * x_m[1:Nx] / x_sd[1:Nx] )*y_sd

sigma <- z_sigma*y_sd

# Predicted y values

# For now, use the original predictors

if (PREDICT_Y) {

for ( i in 1:N_pred ) {

# y_sd and y_m are both >0, so zyP SHOULD > 0

zy_p[i] ~ T(dt( zbeta0 + sum( zbeta[1:Nx] * zx_pred[i,1:Nx] ), sigma = z_sigma , df=df_n), 0, )

#zy_p[i] ~ dt( zbeta0 + sum( zbeta[1:Nx] * zx_pred[i,1:Nx] ), sigma = z_sigma , df=df_n)#

y_pred[i] <- zy_p[i] * y_sd + y_m

}

}

})


PREDICT_Y = TRUE


params = c( "beta0" ,  "beta" ,  "sigma", 

"zbeta0" , "zbeta" , "z_sigma", "df_n", "logProb_zy")


load ('input.RData')


N = length (Data$zy)

constants= Const, init=Inits)


Cmodel <- compileNimble(model)


if (PREDICT_Y) {

modelConf <- configureMCMC(model, print = TRUE, thin = 1, 

monitors = params, monitors2 = 'y_pred')

} else {

modelConf <- configureMCMC(model, print = TRUE, thin = 1, 

monitors = params)

}

modelMCMC <- buildMCMC(modelConf)

CmodelMCMC <- compileNimble(modelMCMC, project = model)


niter <- 1e4


CmodelMCMC$run(niter)

samples = as.matrix(CmodelMCMC$mvSamples)[5000:10000,]


if (PREDICT_Y) {

yp_samples = as.matrix(CmodelMCMC$mvSamples2)[5000:10000,]

}


#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Log likelihood for WAIC & LOO

#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

ll <- samples[,paste0("logProb_zy[",1:N,"]")]


waic_res = loo::waic (as.matrix (ll))

loo_res = loo::loo (as.matrix (ll))

There isn't a way to use the model with multiple sets of variables in one go.  Instead what you need to do is iterate over the sample, put one set of values into the model, simulate or calculate whatever you need, and copy the results out of the model.  There are two strategies for iterating over a sample.  You can keep the sample in its modelValues object (the way it is stored from the MCMC) and use nimCopy to put values in the model.  Or you can keep it as a matrix and use values(model, nodes) <- some_values to put values in the model. I can send an example soon but not at this moment.
-Perry

On Thursday, June 7, 2018 at 5:18:13 AM UTC-7, pdevalpine wrote:
Hi Seongjeun,

Thanks for the question.

It looks like with PREDICT_Y == TRUE, there is no mixing at all in the model.  I may not be following everything, but it looks like this occurs because Inits$z_sigma is 0, which means all zy_p[i] values are 0 and have logProb_zy_p[i] of Inf, and all logProb_zy[i] are -Inf.  The sampling is never able to get away from this state.  

When PREDICT_Y == FALSE, the initial states still have z_sigma == 0 and all logProb_zy[i] are -Inf.  However, any non-zero value of z_sigma in the first MCMC iteration would be accepted because it would raise the logProb_zy[i] to real values and hence be an infinite improvement.  When PREDICT_Y == TRUE, I think this would be defeated by the logProb_zy_p[i] values of Inf, which would make any change in z_sigma give infinitely worse fit. 

In any case, can you try initializing z_sigma with a value > 0?

It still may not be a good idea to include stochastic posterior predictive nodes, because they will slow your mixing.  One strategy for posterior prediction is to make another nimbleModel for that purpose.  You would then iterate over the posterior sample from the first model, put each set of states into the posterior prediction model, and use it for simulation as needed.  Of course in a simple case like yours, you could also do it more directly.  If you use the mvSamples directly, you can access variables in it by name.

Perry
